title: Creating Separation Between Back-to-Back Meetings
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short piece argues that leaders carry the mood and thinking from one meeting into the next, which undermines their effectiveness when meetings run back to back. The author recommends building a deliberate 3 to 5 minute separation between meetings. What matters is not the activity but that it absorbs complete attention briefly, and that the leader is prepared for it in advance. Music, a short walk, answering one email, outlining the next agenda or memorizing a quotation are offered as examples. The justification is that team members deserve the leader's full attention, and a small habit can reset focus. The tone is practical and habit-oriented, framing the pause as a cheap investment.
points: Emotional carryover between meetings makes leaders less effective with the next group.
A 3 to 5 minute pause is realistic for nearly anyone and is enough to switch gears.
The specific activity matters less than whether it fully occupies attention, and having it prepared ahead helps.
Giving team members a leader's full attention is framed as a duty the reset habit makes possible.
quotes: Leaders too often carry over their moods, feelings, and thinking from one meeting to the next. The ability to focus exclusively on the next meeting topic while still reeling from the last one makes leaders less effective than they should be.
Even a small separation between meetings can do a world of good to help with this problem. When the day requires back-to-back meetings, creating a 3- to 5-minute separation is a powerful practice.
It doesn’t matter so much what it is. The key is to engage in an activity for a very brief time that takes your complete attention. Being prepared for this opportunity is equally important.

Consider the idea of music to create this critical separation. Having music at the ready and then immersing yourself in that music for just a few moments gives your brain the chance it needs to switch gears.

Transitions between meetings are challenging enough without sprinting from one discussion to another. Team members deserve the best of you and all of your attention in the matters they want to discuss.
Some tiny habits really are atomic. It only takes 3-5 minutes to reset your attention and give you a fresh view on what comes next.
